children: An error that resulted in Citigroup
its risk-weighted assets by $35B at its U.K. unit could hinder the bank's years-long effort to resolve regulatory penalties that have weighed on its operations, according to a media report on Monday.
The mistake made at an overseas unit could spur U.S. regulators to question whether consent orders placed on Citi should be lifted soon, Reuters reported, citing analysts and former regulators.

"It’s not a huge error given the size of the bank, but any misstep is ​going to complicate their efforts to escape their consent order," Sheila Bair, a former head of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp., told Reuters. "As a general matter, I think this just reinforces the unreliability of ​models in setting risk-based capital requirements.
Citi CEO Jane Fraser has made it a priority to clean up regulatory penalties that began in 2020. In 2024, the company was

to two regulators for failing to make enough progress in fixing problems after a 2020 consent order imposed a $400M civil penalty and required it to remediate risk management, data quality management, and internal control deficiencies.
Almost a year ago, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

amendment to a 2020 consent order that required the bank to remediate data quality management problems. The original consent order came after the bank had accidentally distributed more than $900M to Revlon lenders, paying the full amount of the loans instead of the interest it intended to remit.
Last month, the company was aiming to submit paperwork needed for regulators to lift the consent orders by the end of this year or in Q1 2027, Reuters said.
"With the event in question occurring during a time period that overlaps with Citi's

own attestation work regarding remediation efforts to lift the consent order, it could plausibly lengthen the duration for the 'sustained effectiveness' test, but it would be unlikely to reset ​the process," Austin Taggart, a banking analyst at Morningstar, told Reuters.
